articles.title: My matting pick won all 90 frames and still flickered more in 89 of 89
articles.excerpt: I don't have hand-pulled ground-truth mattes and won't pay anyone to make them, so I went cheap. I took a public-domain green-screen clip from Wikimedia Commons, kept the three seconds where the prese…
articles.body: If a small client job asks for talking-head clips with the background cut out, I'd want to know before quoting whether a free FFmpeg chroma key is enough or whether I need an AI matting model. So on 2026-11-03 I built a small test, scored both, and got a result that changed how I read my own numbers: the AI matte had a lower error than the chroma key on every one of 90 frames, and it also flickered more on 89 of the 89 frame-to-frame steps. The test I could afford I don't have hand-pulled ground-truth mattes and won't pay anyone to make them, so I went cheap. I took a public-domain green-screen clip from Wikimedia Commons, kept the three seconds where the presenter waves (frames 90 to 179), and used a model's transparent export of those frames as the "known" alpha.

articles.title: Ositrustees: Building a Relative Volume Screener in Python
articles.excerpt: A stock trading three times its usual volume can look unusual. But unusual volume does not automatically mean a bullish signal, a company-specific event or a change in market direction. Before interpr…
articles.body: A stock trading three times its usual volume can look unusual. But unusual volume does not automatically mean a bullish signal, a company-specific event or a change in market direction. Before interpreting the activity, a researcher needs to establish what “usual” means. One practical way to investigate that question is Relative Volume (RVOL): a comparison between observed trading volume and a historical reference. Ositrustees is a financial data and analytical technology platform focused on market screeners, sector monitoring, chart-based research and structured market-data workflows. In this tutorial, we will build a small relative volume screener using Python and pandas, identify instruments showing elevated activity and examine the limitations of the resulting observations.

articles.excerpt: Weren't we supposed to be replaced by AI by now? Or at least work less? AI agents were supposed to take over the world. So when exactly is that going to happen, and why are we still working so much? B…
articles.body: Weren't we supposed to be replaced by AI by now? Or at least work less? AI agents were supposed to take over the world. So when exactly is that going to happen, and why are we still working so much? Because we can't pretend that nothing has changed. Even at my workplace, where data security is valued above pretty much everything else, we're already using AI coding agents. Which, in my opinion, means they're basically everywhere by now. Simple features practically write themselves, and even debugging, including in legacy applications, has become significantly easier. And we're only at the beginning of this revolution! What Happens When AI Can Do Everything? A friend and colleague of mine recently encouraged me to write an article about how to get into AI before it's too late.

articles.body: TL;DR Some Android TV users report that pressing Home on the TV remote now selects the top navigation bar instead of their favorite apps. Reports span NVIDIA Shield TV devices, while our own observations suggest the behavior varies across Android TV hardware. Google hasn’t explained the apparent change, and we’re asking readers to help establish how widespread it is. There’s a special kind of frustration that comes from a button doing exactly what it says, just not what your fingers remember. I’ve always found Memories in Google Photos to be a useful and fun feature that often takes me back to the “good old days.” Whether it’s surfacing old clips of my friends and me from college or images from my first date with my wife, it’s usually great at showing the best moments of my life over the years. articles.body: Ahead of the release of Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto VI , Nintendo is launching its own fall juggernaut: a Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time . The remake, which is releasing 28 years after the launch of the original version on Nintendo 64, has a much more realistic visual style and some modern improvements like a jump button, a way to sprint, full voice acting, and a “Threads of Time” feature that helps you keep track of your progress. But while the game has a new coat of paint, it appears many elements will still remain faithful to the classic N64 release. Nintendo has also launched a special version of the Switch 2 and Switch 2 Pro Controller with Triforce imagery to celebrate the game.

articles.excerpt: The Hubble Space Telescope is healthy but is being pulled down toward Earth by atmospheric drag. NASA is considering options to extend the iconic telescope's work.
articles.body: NASA is reviving discussions to rescue the Hubble Space Telescope, which is operating well but is on track to reenter Earth's atmosphere about six years from now. The agency issued a request for information (RFI) on Oct. 29 for "in-space servicing" capabilities, which could include boosting Hubble's orbit (which is naturally degrading due to atmospheric drag), or even a mission to "enhance its capabilities" in some way. articles.title: Ancient star collisions could explain mysterious Little Red Dots and 'impossible' black holes
articles.excerpt: Collisions between stars in the early universe were common, and this could explain the growth of supermassive black holes and the existence of strange Little Red Dots seen by the James Webb Space Tele…
articles.body: New research suggests that collisions between stars in the early universe were common, which could help explain the rapid growth of supermassive black holes and the existence of strange Little Red Dots seen by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The team behind this research performed simulations of the early universe and found stellar systems were densely packed, leading to stars frequently slamming into each other. While rapid collisions would have destroyed the stars involved, slower collisions would have led to repeated mergers, creating single over-massive stars, which could collapse and form larger-than-usual black holes at the end of their lives. These could be the seeds of the first supermassive black holes.
